chapters.name: 6. NUTRIENT APPLICATION
chapters.label: 6. NUTRIENT APPLICATION
chapters.description:
Applying nutrients to your farm—like manure, compost, or fertilizer—is essential for growing healthy crops. But how and when you apply them matters. 

 

One key approach is the “4R” method: using the Right Source, at the Right Rate, at the Right Time, and in the Right Place. This helps you match nutrients to your crop’s needs while reducing waste and environmental risks. 

 

Check out BC's EFP Reference Guide Chapter 6 for practical tips for managing manure, choosing soil amendments, and planning nutrient applications throughout the year. 

 

Whether you’re growing forage, berries, vegetables, or tree fruit, this chapter helps you make informed decisions that benefit your farm and the land around it.

subchapters.name: Introduction: Nutrient Application
subchapters.label: INTRODUCTION
subchapters.description:
Nutrient Sources and the Environment: what you need to know
 

Why nutrients matter
Plants need nutrients to grow. Those nutrients come from fertilizers, manure, soil amendments, and nitrogen fixed by legumes. Each source behaves differently in soil and water—and each can create risk if over‑applied or poorly managed.

 

Understand the basics
This section explains how nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium work, and why soil pH and salts matter. It also covers secondary nutrients, micronutrients, and metals, plus the difference between nutrient sources and soil conditioners.

 

Watch for problem areas
Learn how to avoid phosphorus build‑up, check amendments for contaminants, and choose the right material for your fields.

 

Plan with confidence
Pair this section with tools like the Nutrient Management Calculator and your EFP Planning Advisor to keep nutrients where crops need them and out of waterways.

 

Nutrient Application: the 4R basics
 

Start with the 4Rs
Right Source, Right Rate, Right Time, Right Place—this section shows how to apply these principles on your farm.

 

Match source to crop and soil
Choose the right product for your crop and conditions.

 

Set a rate you can defend
Use soil tests and realistic yield goals to avoid over‑application.

 

Time it to crop demand
Apply nutrients when plants can use them. Split applications may help for long‑season crops.

 

Place to protect water
Position nutrients so crops get them and waterways don’t.

 

Check your work
Calibrate spreaders and sprayers, and use post‑harvest nitrate tests to see if your plan worked.

 

Know the rules
This section also summarizes B.C. regulations and setbacks for nutrient application.

questions.label: 259. Is nutrient application managed to ensure that nutrient sources do not move off site, enter environmentally sensitive areas, and follow legislated setbacks?
questions.textBelowQuestion:
You must meet these conditions:

  • Use a risk assessment tool, such as the BC ARM Tool, to determine the risk of nutrient loss in runoff within 24 hours of application
  • Avoid application during poor conditions, such as heavy precipitation, strong winds, or water tables near the soil surface
  • Avoid application during periods where crops do not take up nutrients (including having enough storage capacity for manure to store all manure during this period)
  • Observe setbacks and adjust them based on current field conditions, slope, and soil drainage capacity
  • Use vegetative buffers to reduce the risk of nutrient loss in runoff
  • Adjust application to avoid discharge directly into tile drains

questions.label: 263. In High-Precipitation Areas, do you manage nutrient application to reduce the risk of nutrient loss and meet legislative requirements?
questions.textBelowQuestion:
You must meet these conditions for nutrient application in High Precipitation Areas:

 

  • Avoid applying nutrients in November, December, and January
  • Complete a risk assessment (such as the BC ARM Tool) within 24 hours before applying nutrients, showing a ‘Low’ risk of nutrient loss in runoff. Keep a copy of the risk assessment.
  • If applying nutrients to bare soils in the fall:
    • Only apply to silt or clay soils, and
    • Plant a crop before winter

questions.label: 257. Does the farm have an up to date (within the past 5 years) Nutrient Management Plan?
questions.textBelowQuestion:
If your farm is 5 hectares (12 acres) or larger, you need an NMP if:

  • Your farm is in a vulnerable aquifer recharge area and any field has post-harvest nitrate levels of 100 kg/ha (89 lb/ac) or more, OR
  • Your farm is in a phosphorus-affected area and any field has soil phosphorus levels of 100 ppm or more (using the Kelowna test method).
